units.statement: Clinical development of mRNA therapies against solid tumors remains at an early stage, characterized by a predominance of phase I trials, a high proportion of investigator-initiated studies, and geographic concentration of sponsors, with only two phase III trials identified.

Here, we summa- rize the current progress, put forward suggestions for future clinical development and provide data supports for industries and research institutions.

units.statement: The field has undergone notable shifts in delivery systems (from dendritic-cell to lipid-based platforms) and encoding strategies (from fixed tumor antigens to personalized neoantigens), with adjuvant or maintenance therapy and combination treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors emerging as the leading clinical-development orientations, positioning mRNA agents as an adjunct rather than a treatment backbone.

units.statement: Lipid-based delivery platforms, including LNP, LPX, and LPP, accounted for 27 of 57 mRNA agents (47.4%), becoming the mainstream platform after 2015 (27/30, 90.0%), replacing dendritic-cell delivery which was the main platform from 1999 to 2014, because lipid systems offer rapid manufacture, high plasticity, transfection rate, and immunogenicity compared with the laborious ex vivo manipulation of dendritic cells.

units.statement: Fixed tumor antigens were the most common coding category (27 agents, 47.4%), followed by neoantigens (8, 14.0%) and autologous tumor cell antigens (5, 8.8%), with MAGE-A1/A3 and survivin as the most common encoded proteins. Since 2009, neoantigen-based trials have tended to exceed fixed-antigen trials, and representative personalized neoantigen programs (mRNA-4157, BNT-122) have shown promising short-term efficacy, though the reliability of neoantigen prediction and the capacity to encode multiple antigens remain unresolved.
